newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai Jan exports rise, other trade indicators weak.
newsitem.headline: Thai Jan exports rise, other trade indicators weak.

text.p: Thai January exports posted moderate year-on-year growth for the first time since last May but trade and current account deficits widened during the month, a finance ministry source said on Wednesday.

The source said Thailand's balance of payments also moved to an estimated 26.6 billion baht ($1.02 billion) deficit in February from a 24.7 billion baht surplus in January due to market attacks on the baht in the first half of last month.
The senior ministry official said January exports rose about 5.1 percent year-on-year to 115.9 billion baht after falling for seven consecutive months.
Exports declined by 0.2 percent for the whole of 1996 after rising 23.6 percent in 1995.
The official said more Thai canned seafood, shoes, electrical appliances and furniture were shipped out in January but agricultural commodity exports slowed down.
January imports also surged to about 154.9 billion baht as factory demand for petroleum and industrial raw materials escalated, from 139.3 billion baht in December.
January imports were at their highest monthly level since May 1996.
He said the January trade deficit widened sharply to a higher than expected 39.0 billion baht, a high since April 1996 and against 22.3 billion in December.
But the current account deficit, moderated by seasonally higher tourism revenue, widened only slightly to 22.5 billion baht in January from 19.1 billion in December.
Thailand's service account, covering mainly tourist and shipping industries, posted a 16.5 billion baht surplus in January, higher than the 3.2 billion baht surplus in December.

The official said press reports of a review by Moody's Investors Service of long-term Thai debt ratings and market attacks on the baht emerged during the first half of February, prompting the Bank of Thailand to intervene in defence of the currency.
He said the baht attacks sharply tightened money market liquidity with short-term interbank rates ranging 10-30 percent during February 1-14.

The source said, however, that the central bank's tough stand shored up market sentiment on the baht in the second half of last month, helping the high overnight interbank rate to ease to 8.50-26.00 percent.

He said the battered export sector showed no early recovery signs in January with the manufacturing production index estimated to grow only four percent year-on-year, its weakest rate in about 10 years.
